clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Functional Mitral Regurgitation evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Functional Mitral Regurgitation is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes optimizing guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with specialist and renal-function review, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: increasing breathlessness, fatigue, and needing three pillows at night over 6 months

Key HPI features: 6-month history of progressive reduction in exercise tolerance, now becoming breathless when walking 50 metres on level ground. Over the past 2 months, has developed orthopnoea requiring three pillows to sleep without coughing and choking, plus paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea waking him up gasping for air twice a week. Has noticed mild ankle swelling in the evenings. Had a myocardial infarction 8 years ago treated with coronary stents.

Objective/Exam findings: Examine JVP (elevated +4 cm H2O above sternal angle). Cardiac auscultation: displaced apex beat to 6th intercostal space anterior axillary line, high-pitched blowing pansystolic/holosystolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex radiating widely to the left axilla, plus a prominent S3 gallop rhythm. Lung auscultation: bilateral fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles. Bloods: NT-proBNP (interpret using age, renal function, rhythm, and clinical context), U&Es, FBC. ECG: broad anterior Q waves. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) to assess ventricular size, function, and mitral regurgitation.
Relevant background/PMH: prior anterior myocardial infarction (8 years ago), coronary artery bypass/stent history, hypertension, mild chronic kidney disease
Current medications: ramipril 10mg OD, bisoprolol 5mg OD, atorvastatin 40mg ON, aspirin 75mg OD, furosemide 20mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Functional Mitral Regurgitation.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Aortic stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathlessness at rest, or coughing up pink frothy sputum.
management_principles: Optimize guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with specialist and renal-function review; diuretics relieve congestion, while ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor use depends on blood pressure, kidney function, potassium, and contraindications
Urgent echocardiogram to assess left ventricular ejection fraction and mitral regurgitant volume
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 70M with prior MI presents with progressive biventricular heart failure symptoms: exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea (3 pillows), PND, and peripheral oedema over 6 months.
reference_soap.objective: Examine JVP (elevated +4 cm H2O above sternal angle). Cardiac auscultation: displaced apex beat to 6th intercostal space anterior axillary line, high-pitched blowing pansystolic/holosystolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex radiating widely to the left axilla, plus a prominent S3 gallop rhythm. Lung auscultation: bilateral fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles. Bloods: NT-proBNP (interpret using age, renal function, rhythm, and clinical context), U&Es, FBC. ECG: broad anterior Q waves. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) to assess ventricular size, function, and mitral regurgitation.
reference_soap.assessment: Severe chronic functional mitral regurgitation (secondary to left ventricular remodeling/dilation post-anterior MI) leading to decompensated congestive heart failure. DDx: primary degenerative mitral valve disease (myxomatous/prolapse), aortic stenosis, COPD exacerbation, recurrent silent ischaemia.
reference_soap.plan: Optimize guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with specialist and renal-function review; diuretics relieve congestion, while ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor use depends on blood pressure, kidney function, potassium, and contraindications. Urgent echocardiogram to assess left ventricular ejection fraction and mitral regurgitant volume. Cardiology referral for consideration of transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair (e.g., MitraClip) or surgical mitral valve replacement.

learning_objectives: Elicit classical left and right congestive heart failure signs: orthopnoea, PND, elevated JVP, S3 gallop, peripheral oedema
Identify the auscultatory hallmarks of mitral regurgitation: pansystolic apical murmur radiating to the left axilla
Differentiate primary structural mitral regurgitation from secondary functional mitral regurgitation post-myocardial infarction
Formulate the four-pillar guideline-directed medical therapy regimen for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)

teaching.one_liner: A leaking mitral valve sends blood backwards into the lungs, so effort tolerance falls and lying flat becomes difficult.
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest, or coughing up pink frothy sputum

must_ask.say: What could you do six months ago that you can't do now?
How many pillows do you need to sleep comfortably?
Does your heart ever feel irregular or fluttery?
Have you been told you have a murmur, or had a heart scan before?
Have you ever had a heart attack?
Have your ankles been swelling up?

history.answer: I've been feeling more and more short of breath and tired over the last six months. Lately, it has gotten so bad that I need three pillows just to sleep.
It started slowly about six months ago, but it has become much worse over the last two months.
Six months ago I could walk around comfortably, but now I get breathless after walking just fifty meters on flat ground.
The breathlessness is always there whenever I move around. I haven't felt this short of breath since my heart attack eight years ago.
For the past two months I've had to prop myself up on three pillows to sleep without coughing and choking, and I wake up gasping for air twice a week.
Walking or doing light chores brings on the breathlessness right away, but cold air, dust, and food don't affect it.
No, I haven't noticed any wheezing, whistling, or rattling sounds when I breathe.
I get a dry hacky cough when I lie flat, but there is no fever, chills, or phlegm coming up.
No, I haven't had any chest tightness, heaviness, or stabbing pains with breathing.
No, my heart doesn't feel like it is racing, fluttering, or skipping beats.
No, I haven't passed out, blacked out, or felt lightheaded.
No, I have never coughed up any blood or pink frothy spit.
I have noticed mild puffiness around both ankles in the evenings, and my shoes feel a bit tight.
Both ankles swell the same amount, with no calf pain, redness, recent long flights, or bed rest.
I feel worn out and drained all the time, but nobody has told me I look pale and I haven't seen any black stools.
No, I don't get numbness or tingling around my mouth or hands, and it isn't brought on by panic or stress.
Nobody has mentioned a heart murmur before, though they did an ultrasound of my heart right after my heart attack eight years ago.
I had a heart attack eight years ago and got stents put in, but I have never had asthma or lung trouble and don't use inhalers.
I used to smoke half a pack a day for twenty years, but I quit completely eight years ago right after my heart attack.
I worked as a chef in restaurant kitchens until I retired, so I was never exposed to asbestos, dust, birds, or mold.
Aside from my heart attack and stents, I have high blood pressure and mild chronic kidney disease.
I was admitted to the hospital eight years ago for my heart attack and stent procedure, but I've had no other operations.
I take ramipril ten milligrams, bisoprolol five milligrams, aspirin seventy-five milligrams, and furosemide twenty milligrams in the morning, plus atorvastatin forty milligrams at bedtime.
I take all my pills faithfully every day and haven't started any new painkillers or over-the-counter medicines.
No, I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I only have an occasional glass of wine with dinner once or twice a week.
I am a retired chef and I live at home with my wife.
My father had heart trouble in his sixties, but there is no family history of sudden early death or heart valve defects.
I think the damage to my heart muscle from my old heart attack is just catching up with me and getting worse as I get older.
I am terrified that I will wake up choking during the night and be completely unable to catch my breath.
I was hoping you could give me stronger water pills to clear the fluid and check if my stents are still working properly.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and temperature 36.6°C.
Mild tachypnea at rest without visible accessory muscle use; no central or peripheral cyanosis, and no digital clubbing.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are non-icteric.
Jugular venous pulse is elevated, measuring 4 cm above the sternal angle at a 45-degree incline.
No chest wall deformities; the apex beat is hyperdynamic and displaced laterally to the sixth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line.
Resonant to percussion bilaterally across all lung zones.
Bilateral fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles are audible, with no wheezing or rhonchi.
High-pitched blowing pansystolic murmur heard loudest at the cardiac apex radiating widely to the left axilla, plus a prominent S3 gallop rhythm.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended with no guarding or rigidity.
Liver edge is smooth and mildly palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin; spleen is not palpable.
Bilateral 1+ pitting edema is present over both ankles and pretibial areas.
Calves are symmetrical bilaterally without localized swelling, warmth, cord, or calf tenderness.
